intro.data: An adjunction is a perfect pairing between two kinds of arrow. The classic case is CURRYING: a function that takes two things at once, (C, A) → B, is the SAME as a function that takes one thing and returns a function for the other, C → (A → B). On the left are two-at-once functions; on the right, their curried forms (plus one impostor with the arguments mishandled). Match each to its transpose.
intro.alchemy: An adjunction is a perfect pairing between two kinds of step. Here: a process taking two reagents at once, (C, A) → B, is the SAME as one taking one reagent and yielding a process for the other, C → (A → B). On the left, two-at-once processes; on the right, their staged forms (plus an impostor). Match each to its partner.
intro.spellcraft: An adjunction is a perfect pairing between two kinds of working. Here: a working taking two essences at once, (C, A) → B, is the SAME as one taking one and yielding a working for the other, C → (A → B). On the left, two-at-once workings; on the right, their staged forms (plus an impostor). Match each to its partner.
intro.abstract: The adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A gives Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, B^A). Match each h : C×A → B with its transpose ĥ : C → B^A. A non-transpose is offered as a distractor.

goal.data: Match each two-at-once function with its curried form.
goal.alchemy: Match each two-at-once process with its staged form.
goal.spellcraft: Match each two-at-once working with its staged form.
goal.abstract: Pair each h : C×A → B with its transpose ĥ : C → B^A.

context.data: This is the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A — currying. Every function of a pair corresponds to exactly one function returning a function.
context.alchemy: The adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: every two-reagent process corresponds to exactly one staged process.
context.spellcraft: The adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: every two-essence working corresponds to exactly one staged working.

afterSuccess.data: Each two-argument function matched exactly one curried form — that one-to-one correspondence IS the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A. Currying isn't a trick; it's a natural bijection Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, A→B). The impostor reordered its arguments, so it wasn't anyone's transpose. Adjunctions are everywhere two descriptions of the 'same' arrow line up perfectly.
afterSuccess.alchemy: Each two-reagent process matched exactly one staged form — that correspondence is the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, A→B). The impostor mishandled its reagents.
afterSuccess.spellcraft: Each two-essence working matched exactly one staged form — that correspondence is the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, A→B). The impostor mishandled its essences.
afterSuccess.abstract: The bijection Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, B^A) is natural in C and B — that is exactly the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A. Currying/uncurrying are the two directions of the transpose.

reveal.summary: An adjunction F ⊣ G is a natural one-to-one correspondence Hom(F A, B) ≅ Hom(A, G B). Currying is the example (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: a function of a pair is the same as a function returning a function.
reveal.programmerAnalogy: curry: ((c, a) => b)  ↔  (c => a => b)  — the same function, two shapes.
